prompt:
Compute absolute Spearman rank correlations between columns 2 to 8 and columns 9 to 17 and run a two-sided, p < 0.05 significance test on the correlations without correcting for multiple comparisons. Exclude subjects that appear to induce spurious correlations. Plot significant correlations in a matrix using the `plot_correlation_matrix` tool.

DATASET: correlates_common_subjects
  386 subjects. Symptoms + task measures only. Subject-level.
  386 rows, 386 subjects (1.0 rows per subject, subject-level)
  columns 2-8  (symptoms): 7-up, 7-down, GAD-7, BIS, BAS, SHAPS, PSWQ
  columns 9-17 (measures): Acc, Pts, WS, LS, Pers, beta, eta_p, eta_n, kappa
  63 correlations, uncorrected at alpha=0.05 -> ~3.2 false positives expected from noise alone

SUPPORTING TABLES (evidence for deciding who to exclude; they are NOT part of the correlation):
  task_data: 36,540 trial rows (~90/subject): block, trial, choice, rt, accuracy, outcome.
    36,540 rows, 9 columns, 406 subjects; columns: subject, block, trial, correct, choice, key, rt, accuracy, outcome
  survey_data: 406 subjects x per-item survey responses plus per-scale response times.
    406 rows, 60 columns, 406 subjects; columns: subject, gad7_q01, gad7_q02, gad7_q03, gad7_q04, gad7_q05, gad7_q06, gad7_q07, gad7_q08, gad7_rt ...
  metrics_data: 386 subjects x the study's own quality metrics: infreq (failed attention checks), isd, reliability, mahalanobis.
    386 rows, 19 columns, 386 subjects; columns: subject, infreq_gad7, infreq_7u7d, infreq_bisbas, infreq_shaps, infreq, isd, reliability, mahalanobis, gad7_rt ...

WHAT THE COLUMNS MEAN:
  7-up           7 Up mania/hypomania screen (higher = more symptoms)
  7-down         7 Down depression screen (higher = more symptoms)
  GAD-7          Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale
  BIS            Behavioural Inhibition System sensitivity
  BAS            Behavioural Activation System sensitivity
  SHAPS          Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (anhedonia)
  PSWQ           Penn State Worry Questionnaire
  Acc            proportion of correct choices in the reversal-learning task
  Pts            total points earned
  WS             win-stay rate: P(repeat choice | previous trial rewarded)
  LS             lose-shift rate: P(switch choice | previous trial unrewarded)
  Pers           perseveration: repeated choices after contingency reversal
  beta           inverse temperature from the RL model (choice determinism)
  eta_p          learning rate for positive prediction errors
  eta_n          learning rate for negative prediction errors
  kappa          choice-stickiness parameter

trace.thought: Compute absolute Spearman correlations between symptom and task measure columns excluding careless subjects to avoid spurious correlations.
Recompute correlations excluding the 85 subjects flagged as careless to avoid spurious correlations.
Plot the significant correlations matrix after excluding careless subjects to visualize robust symptom-task measure associations.

outcome.final_claim: After excluding 85 subjects flagged as careless based on failed attention checks and other quality metrics, 11 out of 63 symptom-to-task measure correlations remain statistically significant at p < 0.05 uncorrected. Significant correlations include negative associations of 7-up mania symptoms with inverse temperature (beta, rho=-0.26), win-stay rate (WS, rho=-0.22), accuracy (Acc, rho=-0.21), and total points (Pts, rho=-0.17), and positive associations with lose-shift rate (LS, rho=0.22) and learning rate for negative prediction errors (eta_n, rho=0.17). BIS also shows significant negative correlations with beta and WS, and positive with perseveration (Pers). GAD-7 shows weaker but significant correlations with kappa and eta_n. The absolute correlation magnitudes range roughly from 0.13 to 0.26. Before exclusion, 25 correlations were significant, but after exclusion only 11 remain, indicating many prior associations were likely artefacts driven by careless responding. This highlights the importance of quality control in such analyses.
limitations: No correction for multiple comparisons was applied, so some significant correlations may be false positives.
Causal or mechanistic interpretations cannot be made from these cross-sectional correlations.
Generalizability to other samples or tasks is unknown without replication.
Impact of borderline-quality subjects (neither clearly careless nor attentive) was not assessed.
outcome.resolving_measurement: Applying multiple comparison correction methods and replication in independent datasets with similar quality control would clarify robustness and generalizability.
